1:
What occasioned the psalm they answer two ways. Clarke thinks it represents the priests and Levites returned from captivity and united in the service of the sanctuary, and reads three psalms as one subject — the Lord entreated to enter his temple in the first, the order and harmony of the temple service pointed out in this, and all exhorted to watchfulness in the next. He notes that Hebrew, Syriac and Vulgate give it to David while the Septuagint and Arabic prefix no name. Calvin has no doubt it is David's thanksgiving for the peace that succeeded a long and melancholy confusion in the kingdom: when he first came to the throne the larger part of the nation counted him an enemy to the public good, and the feud was so mortal that nothing short of destroying the opposing party seemed to promise peace. The hand of God was wonderfully seen in the concord that followed, when men inflamed with the most violent antipathy cordially coalesced.

Henry defines the thing commended before praising it: not merely that brethren do not quarrel and devour one another, but that they delight in each other with mutual endearments and promote each other's welfare with mutual services. Living asunder is sometimes chosen as the best expedient for keeping peace, and may indeed prevent enmity and strife, but the goodness and the pleasantness belong to dwelling together, and so dwelling in unity as to dwell even as one, having one heart, one soul, one interest. David had many sons by many wives, and Henry guesses he penned the psalm for their instruction — had they learned it, much of the mischief that arose in his family would have been prevented. The tribes had long held separate interests under the Judges, often to their cost, and now that they were united under one head, with the ark fixed among them, he would have them see how much that was for their advantage.

Spurgeon takes the opening word as several commands in one. It is a wonder seldom seen, therefore behold it; it may be seen, being the characteristic of real saints, so fail not to inspect it; it is worthy of admiration, so pause and gaze; it will charm you into imitation, so note it well. He makes much of the doubled how, the psalmist attempting no measure of either the good or the pleasure but inviting us to behold for ourselves. The combination of the two adjectives, he says, is more remarkable than the conjunction of two stars of the first magnitude: for a thing to be good is good, but for it to be pleasant as well is better — and though all men love pleasant things, the pleasure is often evil, whereas here the condition is as good as it is pleasant.

On the word rendered in unity Ellicott would put a different weight. Better, he says, altogether: the Hebrew particle here joined to together is sometimes rendered yea where it should plainly be taken with the adjective to intensify it, exactly as our all does, the common idiom for all two — like the French tous deux and the German alle beide — deciding the matter. Many commentators render it also together and find an emphasis on the gathering for the yearly feasts; the allusion may be there, though it is the purpose of the psalm rather than the form of the expression that suggests it. Augustine hears the verse doing its work in history: so sweet is the sound that even those who do not know the Psalter sing it, and this honeyed melody, of the mind as much as of the hymn, begot the monasteries — a trumpet stirring up the brethren who longed to dwell together, sounding through the whole earth and gathering those who had been divided. Gill adds that Aben Ezra would supply the word thing.
2:
The oil is identified before it is interpreted. Gill and Clarke name it the holy composition Moses was ordered to make of the principal spices — sweet cinnamon, sweet calamus, cassia lignea and olive oil — poured on the heads of kings and priests at their anointing; its odour, Clarke thinks, must have been agreeable, serving as a metaphor for the excellence of brotherly love. Keil and Delitzsch explain why a high priest figures at all: the assertion passes from the community of nature that the word brethren expresses to the outward manifestation answering to it, and since the high priest, in whom the mediatorial office culminates, is chief at a feast, the value of that reunion is expressed by a metaphor from him. They add the distinction the metaphor rests on — Aaron's sons were only sprinkled with the oil, while Aaron was expressly anointed, Moses pouring it upon his head, so that he is called the anointed priest where the rest are merely anointed.

How far the oil ran they follow closely. Clarke observes that it was poured on Aaron's head so profusely as to run down upon his garments, as it is still customary in the east to pour oil until it reaches every limb. Ellicott objects that our version's italics are wrongly inserted, since unity cannot flow down, and renders it literally — like the oil, the good oil, on the head descending upon the beard, Aaron's beard, which was descending to the mouth of his robes. Oil is the standing symbol of joy and festivity and is closely connected with love, but the elaboration points further: though all the priests' garments were sprinkled with the holy oil, it was poured on Aaron's head, so that the description, unpleasing as it is to Western ideas, of the saturation of head, face and beard was actually true. Wesley settles the last word against the obvious reading: the skirts meant are not the lower hem of the sacerdotal garment but its upper opening, as the Hebrew properly signifies.

The dew raises a harder question, Hermon being a hundred miles from Jerusalem. Gill answers by identifying the mountains: Hermon was a high hill beyond Jordan, called Sirion by the Sidonians and Shenir by the Amorites, appearing also as Sion — and that, he says, is the Zion meant here, since the dew of Hermon could never descend on the Zion by Jerusalem, and since that Zion was one mountain where these are many. Clarke takes the same line, citing the verse that calls Mount Sion Hermon, and reports Maundrell that the dew there is so copious that even in dry weather the tents were as wet as if it had rained all night. Ellicott refuses it. The sentence is built exactly like the one before it, so the dew on Zion must be the same dew as that on Hermon, just as the oil on the beard was the same as that poured on the head; nor may the mountains of Zion be taken for the spurs about Hermon, since the closing clause shows Mount Zion itself is intended. He quotes Delitzsch that the feature is drawn from nature after all, an abundant dew, when warm days have preceded, being capable of diversion to Jerusalem by a cold current from the north over Hermon.

Where the blessing falls they agree, and say it shortly. Clarke takes the commanded blessing for everlasting life, and holds that where this unity is God pours out his blessings and gives a long and happy life. Wesley reads the dew as the measure of desirableness — as desirable as the dew on Hermon, nay as that heavenly dew of God's ordinances and graces commanded to fall on Zion and Moriah and the hills about Jerusalem — and glosses the there in a phrase, where brethren live in peace and unity.
